newsitem.title: INDIA: Partners ask India party head to quit over scandal.
newsitem.headline: Partners ask India party head to quit over scandal.

text.p: Communist coalition partners on Monday put pressure on the Janata Dal party of Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, asking its president to resign as chief minister of his state over a corruption scandal.

The scandal blew up last month after the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said it planned to prosecute Laloo Prasad Yadav, chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, and federal minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma.

"Instead of making it a partisan issue..., in the interest of parliamentary democracy, he (Yadav) must step down," Somnath Chatterjee, leader of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), told the lower house, Lok Sabha.

The 10-billion-rupee ($280-million) "fodder" scandal involves alleged siphoning off of animal welfare funds by Bihar officials in collusion with politicians. CBI has said as many as 55 officials and politicians would be prosecuted.
The decade-old scandal surfaced last year after officers discovered what appeared to be excessive withdrawals from the state treasury over a period extending into the mid-1980s.
Yadav, president of Janata Dal, and junior Rural Areas and Employment Minister Varma say they are innocent.
Yadav has stubbornly refused opposition demands that he resign and face trial.

The CBI said at the weekend that it had asked the state governor to give permission for Yadav to be prosecuted on corruption charges. The governor has said he needs time to study the details of a proposed charge-sheet.
The scandal hit Gujral within a fortnight after he was in sworn in as prime minister. The 15-party United Front changed its leader in April to win back parliamentary support from the Congress party.
Analysts said the CBI's request for permission to prosecute will force Gujral to act.
They said the scandal could hurt the image of the Janata Dal, but it need not lead Gujral into a crisis.

The CPI-M is not represented in Gujral's government but is considered a key constituent of the United Front, which was formed after general elections last year to keep the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) out of power.
The CPI-M has 32 of the United Front's 177 lawmakers in the 545-member lower house, where Gujral heads a minority government with vital support from the Congress party.
The Janata Dal has so far not responded to opposition calls. Gujral was attending a summit of the South Asian Association of Regional Cooperation (SAARC) in the Maldives.
"This is an hour of test for Prime Minister Gujral," said Nitish Kumar, leader of the opposition Samata Party.

"So far it has been sparring. Only yesterday it (the CBI's demand) has been delivered, said analyst B.G. Verghese of the Centre for Policy Research (CPR). "Varma has been named. Therefore the PM has to take a view."
"It doesn't mean there is necessarily any strain of a dangerous kind (in the coalition)," he said.
